_help.about: The two always-on HUD readouts (design §L) and the super-meter ring (§S). Both readouts are ON by default and each can be toggled in the settings menu (settings keys: hud.speedometer, hud.clock); they're HUD parts, pinned by default (see parts, pins, modes). Small, quiet, R1a palette; the world has no clocks or dials of its own, these are aids for the player only. Restart the game after editing.
_help.parts: The HUD's readouts are parts, each pinned or not (Hud.PARTS, in this order). Top left, one line each: time (Day N · hh:mm · Morning), moon (its phase, how much is lit, · moon up), mansion (the moon's mansion · its beast), season (the season, or the change under way, · day N of the season). Top right: biome (· the soil), temperature (now · the year's average here), weather (the weather now · mm of rain a year), wind (Wind N m/s from a compass point), elevation (Elevation N m), position (latitude N/S, longitude E/W). And the two dials (speedometer, clock). Each corner's column is only as tall as the parts it shows, so a hidden part leaves no gap, and the clock sits just below the right column. Not parts: Swimming and Above the clouds (shown whenever they apply, at the bottom of the right column), and the health bar, the weapon, the crosshair and the name under it, damage numbers, prompts and subtitles (each keeps its own switch in the settings panel), the F3 debug overlay and the F2 frame times.
_help.pins: A part shows in normal play only if it's pinned. The pins are settings (user://settings.cfg, saved the moment they change): hud.speedometer and hud.clock for the dials (on by default: the settings panel's Speedometer and Clock switches are the same pins) and hud.pin.<part> for the rest (off by default), so a new game shows just the two dials. The numbers here are for pinning (see modes): dim_alpha, an unpinned part; hover_alpha, an unpinned part under the mouse; preview_alpha, the pin mark of the part under the mouse (a faint mark on an unpinned part is what a click gives it; a pinned part's mark fading to it is what a click takes away); mark_color, the pin mark (•), the one warm accent.
_help.modes: Normal play: the pinned parts only. H: the full HUD, every part, pinned or not; H again, the pinned ones only (H doesn't hide anything any more). Pinning: Esc frees the mouse and, while no inventory, settings panel or map is open, every part shows, the pinned ones at full brightness with a pin mark (•) before them, the others dimmed (pins.dim_alpha); the part under the mouse brightens and its mark previews the click; a click on a part pins or unpins it (saved at once) and keeps the mouse free; a click anywhere else takes the mouse back and play goes on, showing what's pinned. A caption at the top centre says so, and the two columns step down a line under it. While pinning the speedometer shows at its bright_alpha even at rest, so you can see it to pin it.
_help.speedometer: Ground/air speed in mph and km/h (dev builds add m/s). It sits dim at alpha dim_alpha below dim_below_mps and brightens toward bright_alpha as speed rises to bright_at_mps (the momentum ceiling), so it only asserts itself when you're moving fast. Its glow warms from glow_cold to glow_warm as the super meter fills. size_px: the numerals. smoothing_s: how quickly the shown number follows the real one. mph_round: the mph readout rounds to this (75 mph at the ceiling, by design).
_help.clock: An old railway pocket watch (design §AQ, from the designer's own watch; until 29 Sept a pilot's watch in HUD blue with dawn/dusk marks): a polished steel case with its crown at 12 (case), a white enamel dial, a minute track round the edge (minute_track: a tick a minute, a square every five), bold black numerals (numerals: all | quarters | none, ticks where there is no numeral), the 24-hour numerals 13-24 small and red inside them (hours_24), black skeleton hands (the hour hand twice round a day, the minute hand once a game hour: 6 real minutes) and a thin red seconds hand (seconds_hand: once a game minute, 6 real seconds). No brand, no dawn or dusk marks. Every figure is drawn cell by cell on the 480-line frame's own pixel grid. size_px: the case's diameter (the crown adds about a tenth above it). alpha: the whole watch. Colours: dial, numerals and hands, the red accent (24-hour numerals, seconds hand, cap), the minute ticks, and the case's steel, its dark edge and its highlight.
_help.super_meter: No third element: the meter shows as a thin ring around the tool's charge gauge (ring_px wide, ring_color), visible only when non-zero, and the speedometer glow warms with it. show_below: hidden when under this share, to keep the screen clean until it means something.
_help.text: Every HUD and UI font: an early-computer / typewriter face — monospaced, slightly uneven, like a teletype or an 8-bit console font — never a clean modern sans. font: the font file under assets/fonts (a free monospaced typewriter-style TTF; fallback: the engine monospace). Design §Y: the HUD is drawn INSIDE the 480-line internal frame and upscaled with it, so every px size in this file is at the 480 reference and text is automatically chunky and the right size at any window; scale_by_height is off (the upscale does the scaling). base_px: the body size at 480 lines (2026-09-28: raised from 9 to 11 — 9 was hard to read once upscaled; the prompt line and the crosshair name are larger still). 2026-09-29 (from play: still hard to read): font is now VT323 (a DEC terminal face, SIL OFL), drawn without antialiasing on its own 10 px grid, and every size snaps to crisp_px (20 body, 40 headings) so no glyph falls between pixels; base_px 20. 2026-09-30 (Mike: bigger, more legible): base_px 30, the prompt and names 30, the small readouts 20; VT323 is crisp at multiples of 10. The typewriter face stays in assets/fonts. 6 Oct, design §ES (Claude Code): the frame is 270 lines by default, so every size here (still at the 480 reference, ref_height_px) is scaled by the frame's lines over 480 before it snaps to crisp_px (HudText.scale()): 0.5625 at 270, where body text lands on 20 px and the small readouts on VT323's own 10 px grid (10 added to crisp_px); switching the pixel size (F11, Settings) re-sizes it live.
_help.layout: Where the readouts sit: corner (top_left, top_right, bottom_left, bottom_right), margin_px from the edges. The health meter keeps its own place (data/combat.json feedback.meter).
_help.reticle: The crosshair (first person, or while aiming): size_px at the 480 reference (design §Y), thickness_px, gap_px, color. A bit larger than before, per §W. 7 Oct, design §EX.7 (Claude Code): one crosshair for both games (Reticle; the open world's StatusHud and the crawler draw it with the same code). It is drawn cell by cell on the frame's own pixel grid round the frame's middle pixel: four arms, each size_px / 2 long and thickness_px wide, starting gap_px clear pixels out from the middle pixel, each on a one-pixel dark edge (navy at 70%). Like every size in this file it is scaled by the frame's lines over 480 and rounded to whole pixels, never under one (480 lines: arms 5, gap 3, width 1; 270: arms 3, gap 2, width 1). The crawler shows it too (crawler.json hud), and there the Settings switch Crosshair dot (hud.reticle) hides it. hit_marker (Mike, 7 Oct: "if you get a hit on a creature tho, there will be an X shape in the diagonal spaces between the regular crosshair to signify a successful hit"; Claude Code's first guesses for the numbers; Reticle.hit, x_cells): when your lit swing meets a creature (its strike staggered or its body caught) or your fire pot's burst catches one, an X shows for show_s seconds: four short diagonals in the corners between the arms, from from_px to from_px + length_px - 1 pixels out along each diagonal from the middle (at the 480 reference, scaled like the arms), as wide as the arms, in their colour on the same dark edge. The crosshair never warms or marks what you can light (Mike, 7 Oct: that is for the player to figure out).
_help.plant_name: The genus/species readout for the plant under the reticle: shown only within reach_m of it (about a metre, design §W); nothing beyond that. Two lines: the binomial at name_px, then the common name and where on Earth it comes from (the entry's `origin`, or the first clause of its research note) at origin_px. Sizes are at the 480-line reference like everything else here.
_help.log: Design 30 Sept §AZ: Enter opens the log (Minecraft-chat style, in the 480-line frame), newest at the bottom, every line stamped from the clock in game time. events lists what gets a line; the text box takes a note (note_max_chars). Esc closes. Persists per world.
_help.pins_ambient: Design 30 Sept §AU: the pins that start pinned in the ambient movement profile (walking never lights the speedometer).

calendar._help: (design §DD, wired: World.calendar, clock_text, stamp_text) The year joins the day count (Mike, 3 Oct: "instead of just having day one, day two, we could have like day one of year whatever"). The time line (parts: time) and the log's stamps read time_format: day is 1-365 within the year and year counts from the world's first day, so a new world opens on Day 1 of Year 1 (§CG) and the day still turns at local midnight where you stand, as built. day = ((day count - 1) mod year_days) + 1, year = floor((day count - 1) / year_days) + 1. Placeholders: {day}, {year}, {hh}, {mm}. year_days comes from data/sky/day_cycle.json. A year is 876 hours of play (tools/reference/moon_reference.py), so most worlds stay in Year 1: the year is deep time more than a counter. year_names: how a year is named, 'number' until Mike chooses (he raised the zodiac; the twelve animals, the four beasts of the mansions, or names of our own are the options). The lunar side is built already: the moon line (phase, how much is lit, moon up) and the mansion line (the moon's mansion and its beast, the 28 mansions drawn beside the moon) are parts you can pin (Esc, then click). log_stamp: the log's own stamp (§AZ), shorter.

log_more._help: [NOT WIRED YET — given (a thing a stranger hands you; nothing gives yet)] Wired: found (§DE, kind found), spoken (§DJ), scroll, shown, asked and deciphered (§DK, Shrines; the log panel wraps a long entry so it shows whole), tome (§DL: "You found a tome: <title>"). What else the log keeps (§AZ: each line stamped, kept per world). found: waking at a fire after you were taken (camps.json wake_found). spoken: a line from one of the few who speak (§DJ). given / asked: what a stranger gave you, or would like fetched. scroll: the sealed scroll taken (shrines.json log); shown: someone who can't read it hands it back; deciphered: the reader's question and then the scroll's whole text, kept whole (keep_deciphered_whole) so you can read it back any time (Mike: "it should probably be in the log that you could reference back to"). tome: a tome found; its pages are read from the item while you carry it (§DL). The lines are data where they are fixed (camps.json, shrines.json) and come from the speaker or the scroll where they are not. Never a quest log: no objectives, no markers, no list of things to do.
